cards.explanation: The answer is that he does what is evil. Verse 2 doesn't dance around it. Zedekiah, the king of Judah, "…did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as Jehoiakim had done." Jehoiakim was an earlier king of Judah. Crown on his head, throne under him, and that's the verdict. The chapter tells you early what kind of story this is, friends.

The answer is True. Verse 3 says it right there: "…Zedekiah also rebelled against the king of Babylon." Evil in the sight of the LORD, and now he's picking a fight with Babylon too. That's a lot to put on one king's schedule, friends. And the next verse shows what comes of it.

The answer is a siege wall. Verse 4 says Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, "…encamped outside the city and built a siege wall all around it." All around, friends. Jerusalem was ringed in. Then verse 5 says the city was kept under siege until Zedekiah's eleventh year.

The answers are eleventh and famine. Verse 5 says the city "…was kept under siege until King Zedekiah’s eleventh year." That lines up with verse 1, where Zedekiah reigned eleven years. Think about that, friends. We're talking years under siege, not a long weekend. Verse 6 says "…the famine in the city was so severe that the people of the land had no food." It's a hard line, so I'll say it plainly and leave it there.

The answer is that they flee the city by night. Verse 7 says "…all the men of war fled the city by night…" They went by the gate between the two walls near the king's garden. The Chaldeans, Babylon's army, had the city surrounded, and they ran anyway.

The answer is False. Verse 8 says "…the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho…" Zedekiah went out by night toward the Arabah, but the Chaldeans came after him. They caught him, friends.

The answer is that his whole army deserts him. Verse 8 says, "…his whole army deserted him." The whole army, friends. The king runs out by night with his men, and in the plains of Jericho, he's on his own. That's a lonely spot to be in.

The answer is Riblah. Verse 9 says the Chaldeans "…brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath…" That's where the king pronounced judgment on Zedekiah. Riblah comes up again later in the chapter, so keep an eye out, friends.

The answer is True. Verse 11 says the king of Babylon took Zedekiah to Babylon, "…where he kept him in custody until his dying day." It's a heavy verse, friends. I think this one hurts. Let's sit with it for a moment.

The answer is that he burns it down. Verse 13 says Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, "…burned down the house of the LORD…" That's the temple, friends. It's a sad line, and it's right there in the text.

The answer is False. Verse 13 says Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem. The text adds, "…every significant building." Nothing on that list was spared, friends.

The answer is breaks down. Verse 14 says the whole army of the Chaldeans "…broke down all the walls around Jerusalem." That's the same city that had been shut in by a siege wall. Now its own walls come down, friends.

The answer is that he carries them into exile. Verse 15 says Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, "…carried into exile…" some of the poorest people and those who remained in the city. The deserters and the craftsmen go too. Exile means leaving home behind, friends.

The answer is False. In verse 15, Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, carried into exile "…the deserters who had defected to the king of Babylon…" along with others. Defecting didn't keep them home, friends. They went with the rest.

The answer is True. Verse 16 says Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, "…left behind some of the poorest of the land to tend the vineyards and fields." So the land still had people on it, working the vineyards and fields. Not everyone was carried off, friends.

The answer is that he pardons him and frees him from prison. Verse 31 says Evil-merodach, the new king of Babylon, "…pardoned Jehoiachin king of Judah and released him from prison." Pardoned, and let out. After all the fire and ruin, a door opens, friends.

The answer is kindly. Verse 32 says Evil-merodach, the king of Babylon, "…spoke kindly to Jehoiachin…" Kindly, friends. After a pardon and an open prison door, the king's words are kind too. That's a good turn in this chapter.

The answer is at the king's table. Verse 33 says Jehoiachin "…dined regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life." He changed out of his prison clothes and took a seat at the king's table. Regularly, friends. That's a standing seat.

The answer is False. Verse 34 says the king of Babylon provided Jehoiachin a daily portion "…for the rest of his life, until the day of his death." It's no one-year deal, friends. It's every day, for as long as he lived.
